newsitem.title: USA: NY state bill would curb rights on CEO pay - AFL-CIO.
newsitem.headline: NY state bill would curb rights on CEO pay - AFL-CIO.

text.p: A bill in the New York State Senate would make it easier to raise the compensation of top corporate officers by restricting shareholder rights to approve executive stock options, the AFL-CIO said Tuesday.

A section of a bill pending in the state Senate would end a requirement that shareholders approve the granting of rights or stock options to directors or officers of companies chartered in the state, the 78-union federation said.

"The legislation eliminates existing checks over executive compensation packages which often bestow incredible riches on top managers with little regard to company performance or stockholder value," AFL-CIO Secretary-Treasury Richard Trumka said in a letter to state Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno.

Trumka said the provision is of concern to the labour federation, whose unions have officers who serve as trustees on jointly administered pension funds and government employee retirement systems that invest in stocks and "put a premium on management accountability and building long-term value."
The labour federation asked Bruno, a Republican, to keep the measure from coming to a vote in the New York Senate in Albany until the section to which it objects is removed.

Neither federal law, nor the state law of Delaware, where most companies are incorporated, requires shareholder approval for the granting to stock options to top corporate executives or directors, according to Rich Ferlauto, a special projects coordinator in the AFL-CIO's Office of Investment.

The chief executives of the 34 S&P 500 companies chartered in New York State had stock option wealth last year that averaged $15.3 million, had a median value of $5.7 million and totalled $520.2 million, the AFL-CIO said.

Topping the list was General Electric Co. CEO John Welsh with $122.7 million in stock compensation, International Business Machine Corp. CEO Louis Gersterner, with $102 million, and American Express Co. CEO Harvey Golub with $42.6 million, the report said.
Ferlauto acknowledged that the value of stock option packages, which are often based on complicated formulas, has been enhanced in part by rising stock prices.
But, he added, "What we're pointing out here is that the degree of compensation has actually skyrocketed past the market performance."
